newsitem.title: CHINA: FEATURE-HK husbands take cross-border concubines.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-HK husbands take cross-border concubines.

text.p: In China, it's a practice as old as time. In the late 20th century it's not exactly the done thing, but it's a fact the concubine is back in vogue.
Thousands, possibly tens of thousands, of Hong Kong men are believed to have succumbed to the temptation and found concubines across the border, social workers say.
Some are truck drivers, technicians, or factory foremen, others managers or business executives on assignment in China.
A by-product of the booming cross-border business between China and its newest region, Hong Kong, they all go there for the same reason. To earn a living and provide for their family.
They probably return to see their families only once a week at best, some just once every two or three months. They often bring back a bundle of troubles.
BOREDOM, NEED FOR LOVE, DRIVE MEN TO CONCUBINES
The problem, entrenched for years, is a heartache with which many in the territory of 6.4 million people can identify.
Local television serials dramatise the problem during prime time and victims -- wives of some of these philandering men -- often pour their hearts out on late night radio chat shows.
The Catholic Caritas Family Service says boredom, isolation, sexual craving and the need for motherly care, drive many Hong Kong men who work in China to seek a second wife.

"Taking a concubine there has become a social norm. It's so easy, they have so many choices," said Caritas supervisor Eliza Lam, adding that wives usually had scarcely any idea what their husbands were up to while stationed across the border.
The wives in Hong Kong are almost all housewives dedicated to their homes and children, and suffer a big shock when they discover their husbands have concubines in China.
"Most of them sense there is a problem when their husbands start bringing home less money and paying less attention to the family, especially to the children," Lam said.
HONG KONG WIVES BECOME VICTIMS
The disruption caused to affected families is severe.
The husbands, usually the family's sole breadwinner, often threaten to stop giving money to the wives and force them to accept their relationships with concubines, Lam said.
"Lesser-educated housewives or wives incapable of being independent cave in, in a trade-off for the husband's financial contribution to the family," Lam said.

One victim, a 36-year-old housewife married for 12 years and a mother of two, who gave her name as Miss Ng, said she had discovered her husband had a concubine in China just three months after a new child was born into the family.
When she found out, her husband demanded a divorce.

"He wanted me to divorce him without letting his parents and the children know and he wanted me to continue taking care of the children, so he could marry the woman in China without committing bigamy," Ng said.
Ng, who refused to divorce her husband, said her husband did not give her a cent for two years. A woman with little education, she was struggling to support the whole family.
Ng said the 24-year-old mainland concubine had been forcing her 40-year-old husband to divorce in order to come to Hong Kong, and planned then to take the children, too.

Ng said she knew many women in similar tragedies and that mainland concubines saw their liaisons as a ticket to Hong Kong. "Ten out of ten of these men who work on the mainland keep concubines. And many of the mainland women ask for divorces within months of getting residency here," she said.
CHILDREN GROW UP HATING FATHERS WITH CONCUBINES
Hong Kong's divorce rate has almost tripled since 1982, from 0.67 to 1.86 per 1000 persons, but it is unclear if the concubine problem has influenced this trend.
A Caritas study of 421 cases, involving 866 children, of whom two thirds were under 12 years old, showed children will grow up hating their father and his concubine.
"The innocent children will protect the mother and be very sympathetic to her. They will feel deprived of fatherly love, material needs, lose confidence and feel insecure," Lam said.
Lam believed that after the children grow up, they may lack confidence in marriage because of their family's experience.
And for some others, they may perpetuate the ugly circle. "Some would repeat their father's history." Lam said.

But she thinks the problem of cross-border, extramarital affairs should be easier to solve than local cases. "If the husbands quit their jobs in China, the affairs come to an end because in most cases it's a question of sex, not love."
